    All in One View

    Content from Introduction to microbiome data

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is microbiome data?
    • How is microbiome data produced?
    • What will we learn to do with it in this lesson?

    Objectives

    • Describe the steps of a microbiome study, and point out which steps this lesson covers.
    • Name the four parts of a microbiome dataset.
    • Explain why we compare proportions instead of raw read counts.
    • State the research question of the study used in this lesson, and name factors other than the disease that could affect the answer.

    What is a microbiome?

    Our bodies, as well as soil, oceans and plants, are home to huge communities of microorganisms: bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses. Such a community, together with its environment, is called a microbiome.

    The gut microbiome helps us digest food, trains our immune system and protects us from pathogens. Changes in the gut microbiome have been linked to many diseases, including colorectal cancer, which is the topic of our example study.

    To study a microbiome, we need to know who is there and how much of each. This is what microbiome sequencing measures.

    The microbiome data science workflow

    A microbiome study goes through the same steps from start to finish. The figure below shows them as a workflow, from top to bottom.

    Figure: microbiome data science workflow. Source: OMA.

    First, the data is produced:

    • Data generation: a study system, such as people, animals or soil, is sampled. The DNA of each sample is sequenced, which gives the raw data: millions of short DNA sequences, called reads.
    • Pre-processing: specialized tools clean the reads, group them and find out which taxa (groups of related organisms, such as species) they come from. The result is a set of tables.

    Then the tables are analysed, in five numbered steps:

    1. Data object: the tables (abundance table, taxonomy, sample metadata and tree) are imported into R and stored together in one object.
    2. Data processing: the data is checked, summarized at different taxonomic levels (agglomeration) and transformed.
    3. Statistical analysis: we answer the research question, for example with alpha diversity, beta diversity and differential abundance analysis.
    4. Data integration: the microbiome is combined with other data types measured from the same samples, such as metabolites.
    5. Results: we report what we found, in a reproducible way.

    This lesson covers the analysis of a single abundance table: steps 1–3, highlighted in the figure below. The R/Bioconductor packages that we use, from the OMA framework, are made for these steps. Data generation and pre-processing have already been done for us with other tools; episode 2 introduces them and what to keep in mind about them. Combining several tables (step 4) is the topic of a follow-up lesson, the multi-omics lesson.

    At the start of each episode, the same figure shows where we are in the workflow.

    From a sample to a table

    Two sequencing approaches are common:

    • Amplicon sequencing (e.g. 16S rRNA) reads one marker gene. It is cheap and tells us mainly which bacteria are present.
    • Shotgun metagenomics reads all DNA in the sample. It gives a more detailed picture, often down to species, and also tells us about genes and functions.

    The data in this lesson come from shotgun metagenomics. The reads were compared with a database of marker genes by a tool called MetaPhlAn, which reports how much of each species is in each sample.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Which steps does this lesson cover?

    Which of these tasks belong to this lesson? For the others, say where they happen instead.

    1. Collecting stool samples and sequencing their DNA.
    2. Running MetaPhlAn on the sequencing reads.
    3. Importing the abundance table into R.
    4. Testing whether diversity differs between people with and without cancer.
    5. Combining the microbiome with metabolite measurements of the same people.

    Tasks 3 and 4 belong to this lesson (data object and statistical analysis). Tasks 1 and 2 are data generation and pre-processing; they were done before we received the data. Task 5 is data integration, the topic of the multi-omics lesson.

    The parts of a microbiome dataset

    Whatever the sequencing approach, the result is a set of related tables. Here is a small made-up example with four taxa and three samples:

    Abundance table: how many reads of each taxon were found in each sample.

    Sample 1 Sample 2 Sample 3
    Bacteroides 500 120 0
    Prevotella 0 800 900
    Faecalibacterium 300 60 80
    Escherichia 200 20 20

    Taxonomy: where each taxon belongs in the tree of life.

    Phylum Family Genus
    Bacteroides Bacteroidota Bacteroidaceae Bacteroides
    Prevotella Bacteroidota Prevotellaceae Prevotella
    … … … …

    Sample information (also called metadata): what we know about each sample.

    Disease Age Location
    Sample 1 CRC 61 Bhopal
    Sample 2 healthy 45 Bhopal
    Sample 3 healthy 38 Kerala

    Phylogenetic tree: how closely the taxa are related to each other.

    In the next episodes, we will store all of these together in a single R object.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Which part of the dataset do you need?

    For each question below, decide which part of the dataset (abundance table, taxonomy, sample information or phylogenetic tree) you need to answer it. Some questions need more than one part.

    1. How many Prevotella reads were found in Sample 2?
    2. Is Prevotella more common in healthy people than in people with CRC?
    3. What share of Sample 1 belongs to the phylum Bacteroidota?
    4. Are the taxa in Sample 1 more closely related to each other than the taxa in Sample 3?
    1. The abundance table only.
    2. The abundance table and the sample information (to know who has CRC).
    3. The abundance table and the taxonomy (to know which taxa belong to Bacteroidota). In the toy example, Bacteroides and Prevotella are both Bacteroidota, so the share is 500 / 1000 = 50 %.
    4. The abundance table (which taxa are in each sample) and the phylogenetic tree (how related they are).

    Most analyses combine several parts. This is why, in episode 4, we store them together in one object.

    Two things to keep in mind

    The numbers are relative

    The number of reads we get from a sample depends on the sequencing machine and on how many samples were sequenced together. It does not depend on how many bacteria were in the gut. This total number of reads per sample is called the library size (or sequencing depth). In our study, the library sizes range from 3.3 to 27.7 million reads.

    Look at Sample 1 above: it has 1000 reads in total. If we had sequenced it twice as deep, every number would double, but the community would be exactly the same. This is why we usually compare proportions (relative abundances) rather than raw counts. In Sample 1, Bacteroides makes up 500 / 1000 = 50 % of the community.

    Proportions bring their own catch. They always add up to 100 %, so if one taxon grows, the shares of all the others shrink, even if their real amounts did not change. Data like this is called compositional. In episode 5, we use a transformation (rclr) that is designed for compositional data.

    There are lots of zeros

    Most taxa are found in only a few samples. In our study dataset, 84 % of the abundance table is zeros. Some zeros mean that a taxon is truly absent; others mean that it was too rare to be detected.

    These two properties, relative (compositional) numbers and many zeros, are why microbiome data needs methods that are designed for it.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: More reads, more bacteria?

    Sample A has 10 000 reads of Escherichia coli and sample B has 20 000 reads of E. coli.

    1. Can you conclude that sample B contains more E. coli than sample A?
    2. What else would you need to know?
    1. No. Sample B might have been sequenced more deeply.
    2. You need the total number of reads (library size) of each sample. For example, if sample A has 100 000 reads in total and sample B has 400 000, then E. coli makes up 10 % of sample A but only 5 % of sample B.

    Our study: the gut microbiome in colorectal cancer

    Throughout this lesson, we analyse data from Gupta et al. (2019). The researchers collected stool samples from 60 people in India:

    • 30 people with colorectal cancer (CRC)
    • 30 healthy people

    The samples were sequenced with shotgun metagenomics. After pre-processing, the abundance table has 308 species and 60 samples: many more taxa than samples, which is typical for microbiome data. For each person, we also know their age, gender and where they live: Bhopal (a city in central India) or Kerala (a state in southern India).

    Our research question is:

    Is the gut microbiome of people with colorectal cancer different from that of healthy people, and which bacteria differ?

    Challenge

    Challenge 4: What else could differ?

    We want to compare people with CRC to healthy people. Apart from the disease, what else could make their microbiomes differ? Why might it matter where each person lives?

    Write down your ideas before you look at the solution. In a workshop, share them with the other learners, for example in the shared notes.

    Diet, age, medication, lifestyle and geography all affect the gut microbiome. If, for example, most healthy people came from one place and most CRC patients from another, we could not tell whether a difference is caused by the disease or by the place. Such a mix-up of two variables is called confounding. We check our data for it in episode 4.

    Where are we heading?

    Episode 2 introduces data generation and pre-processing, and episode 3 sets up the project. After that, each episode answers one part of our research question:

    Episode Topic Question
    4 Data object What is in our data?
    5 Data processing Which bacteria dominate the samples?
    6 Alpha diversity Do the groups differ in diversity within samples?
    7 Beta diversity Do the groups differ in overall composition? Are there natural groups of samples?
    8 Differential abundance and prevalence Which bacteria differ?
    9 Machine learning How well can we predict an outcome, here the disease, from the microbiome?
    10 Capstone Can you do the whole analysis yourself, on new data?

    Alpha diversity, beta diversity and differential abundance are the analyses that most microbiome studies report. For some studies they are all that is needed. When a study goes further, for example with machine learning or multi-omics, these analyses are still the first steps for understanding the data.

    We will use packages from the OMA framework, a set of R/Bioconductor packages for microbiome data science. When you want to learn more after this lesson, the online book Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis (OMA) covers all of these topics in more depth.

    Key Points
    • A microbiome study goes from data generation and pre-processing to the data object, data processing and statistical analysis. This lesson covers the data object, data processing and statistical analysis steps; data integration is covered in the follow-up multi-omics lesson.
    • Microbiome data consists of an abundance table (taxa × samples), taxonomy, sample information and often a phylogenetic tree.
    • The number of reads per sample depends on sequencing depth, so we usually compare relative abundances.
    • Relative abundances are compositional: they add up to 100 %, so a change in one taxon changes the shares of all others.
    • Microbiome data contains many zeros and many more taxa than samples.
    • Alpha diversity, beta diversity and differential abundance are the standard first analyses of a microbiome study, and for some studies they are enough.
    • This lesson follows one study, on colorectal cancer, from data to results. Other differences between the groups, such as where people live, can confound the comparison.

    Content from From samples to tables

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 40 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • Where do the samples come from, and what should we keep in mind about them?
    • How do sequencing reads become the tables that we analyse in R?
    • How do I import the output of these pipelines into R?

    Objectives

    • Name steps of data generation that can affect the results, such as sample storage, DNA extraction and batches.
    • Describe the main steps of amplicon and shotgun pre-processing pipelines.
    • Match the outputs of a pipeline to the parts of a TreeSummarizedExperiment.
    • Choose the mia function that imports the output of a given pipeline.

    Where are we?

    Before any analysis in R, samples must be collected and sequenced (data generation), and the raw sequencing reads must be turned into tables (pre-processing). Pre-processing is usually run on the command line, with tools made for this purpose. The R/Bioconductor packages of the OMA framework start after these steps, from the tables.

    In this lesson, these steps have already been done for us. This short episode explains what happens to the samples before we receive the data, what to keep in mind about it, and how you can bring the output of your own pipeline into R.

    Data generation: from a sample to reads

    The analysis can only be as good as the samples. Many choices are made before any data reaches R, and each of them can leave a mark on the data:

    • Study design. Which groups are compared, and how many samples are collected? Information about the samples, such as age, diet, medication (especially antibiotics) and place of living, is collected at the same time. We need it later to interpret the results.
    • Sampling and storage. How a sample is collected, how long it waits at room temperature and how it is stored (for example frozen) can change its microbial composition.
    • DNA extraction and library preparation. The DNA is extracted from the sample and prepared for sequencing. Extraction kits differ, for example in how well they break open different bacteria, so the same sample can give different compositions with different kits.
    • Batches. Samples are often processed and sequenced in batches. Samples of the same batch tend to be more similar to each other (a batch effect). If all samples of one study group are in one batch, the batch and the group cannot be told apart. Mixing the groups across batches avoids this.
    • Controls. Negative controls (samples without any material) reveal contamination from the lab and the reagents. This matters most for samples with few bacteria, such as skin or tissue. Positive controls (mock communities with known composition) show how accurate the whole process is.

    Finally, a sequencer reads short pieces of DNA, called reads, and writes them into FASTQ files: one sequence and its quality scores per read. A single sample typically gives tens of thousands (amplicon) to tens of millions (shotgun) of reads.

    In our study, stool samples were collected from people with colorectal cancer and healthy people in two places in India, and sequenced with shotgun metagenomics (Gupta et al. 2019). The paper describes how the samples were collected and processed. When you analyse a dataset, always read this part of the methods: it tells you which variables, such as batches or locations, you may need to take into account.

    Pre-processing: from reads to tables

    The reads are not yet a table of taxa; a pipeline must first find out which organism each read comes from.

    Amplicon sequencing (e.g. 16S rRNA) Shotgun metagenomics
    What is sequenced One marker gene All DNA in the sample
    Main steps Quality control and trimming → grouping reads into ASVs or OTUs → assigning taxonomy with a reference database (e.g. SILVA, GTDB) → building a tree Quality control → removing host (human) reads → taxonomic profiling with marker genes → functional profiling
    Common tools DADA2, QIIME 2, mothur MetaPhlAn (taxa), HUMAnN (genes and pathways)

    ASVs (amplicon sequence variants) are groups of identical reads, and OTUs (operational taxonomic units) are groups of very similar reads. In amplicon data, they are the rows of the abundance table, in the same way as the species are the rows in our data.

    DADA2 is itself a Bioconductor package, so amplicon pre-processing can also be done in R. Shotgun tools such as MetaPhlAn and HUMAnN run on the command line.

    What are the numbers in the table?

    To find out which taxon a read (or an ASV) comes from, the pipeline compares its sequence with a reference database of known sequences. The reads assigned to each taxon are then summarized per sample. Depending on the tool, the abundance table holds the number of reads of each taxon, or each taxon’s share of the sample (relative abundance).

    Whatever the tool, the numbers tell us about the sequenced DNA, not directly about the number of bacteria in the gut. The total of a sample depends on how deeply it was sequenced. This is why we transform the data before comparing samples (episode 5).

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: From samples to tables

    1. Put these steps of an amplicon pipeline in order: assign taxonomy, quality control and trimming, build a tree, group reads into ASVs.
    2. You open a shotgun abundance table and see that every column sums to 100. What kind of numbers does it hold? Can you tell from the table how many reads each sample had?
    3. In a study, all samples of patients were sent to the sequencing facility in January and all samples of healthy controls in March. In March, the facility switched to a new DNA extraction kit. What could go wrong in the analysis?
    1. Quality control and trimming → group reads into ASVs → assign taxonomy → build a tree.
    2. Relative abundances, in percent. No: the number of reads is not visible. You need it from elsewhere, for example the sample information.
    3. The extraction kit (a batch effect) and the study group are mixed up. Any difference between patients and controls could be caused by the kit, and no analysis can tell the two apart afterwards. Mixing the groups across batches when the samples are processed avoids this.

    Where do the outputs go in R?

    In R, we store all outputs of a pipeline in one object of the TreeSummarizedExperiment class (TreeSE for short), which we build in episode 4. It has a place for each output:

    • assay: the abundance table, with taxa as rows and samples as columns.
    • rowData: information about the rows (taxa), such as the taxonomy.
    • colData: information about the columns (samples).
    • rowTree: a tree that connects the rows.
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Where does each output go?

    A colleague ran an amplicon pipeline and sent you these files. In which part of a TreeSummarizedExperiment (assay, rowData, colData or rowTree) would each one go?

    1. A table with the number of reads of each ASV in each sample.
    2. A table that gives the phylum, family and genus of each ASV.
    3. A spreadsheet with the age, sex and treatment group of each mouse.
    4. A Newick file that describes how the ASVs are related.
    5. A file with the raw reads of each sample (FASTQ).
    1. assay: the abundance table, with ASVs as rows and samples as columns.
    2. rowData: information about the rows (taxa).
    3. colData: information about the columns (samples).
    4. rowTree: the phylogenetic tree of the rows.
    5. Nowhere. Raw reads are the input of the pipeline; the TreeSE holds its output.

    Importing pipeline output into R

    In episode 4, we build a TreeSE from plain tables, so that we see each part. For the output of the common pipelines, the mia package has ready-made functions that build the TreeSE directly:

    Source Function
    QIIME 2 (.qza files) importQIIME2()
    DADA2 (in R) convertFromDADA2()
    mothur importMothur()
    BIOM files importBIOM()
    MetaPhlAn importMetaPhlAn()
    HUMAnN importHUMAnN()
    taxpasta (standardized output of many shotgun profilers) importTaxpasta()
    phyloseq objects convertFromPhyloseq()

    For example, importing a MetaPhlAn table or a QIIME 2 feature table looks like this (the file names are placeholders):

    R 

    tse <- importMetaPhlAn(file.path("data", "metaphlan_merged.txt"))

tse <- importQIIME2(
    assay.file = file.path("data", "table.qza"),
    row.file = file.path("data", "taxonomy.qza"),
    col.file = file.path("data", "sample-metadata.tsv"),
    tree.file = file.path("data", "rooted-tree.qza")
)

    Many public shotgun datasets, including the one used in this lesson, are also available as TreeSE objects directly from the curatedMetagenomicData package.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Which import function?

    Which function would you use in each case?

    1. You received a .biom file from a sequencing facility.
    2. Your previous analysis was done with the phyloseq package, and you have the phyloseq object saved in an .rds file.
    3. You profiled shotgun samples with MetaPhlAn and merged the outputs into one table.
    4. You profiled the same shotgun samples with HUMAnN to get pathway abundances.
    1. importBIOM().
    2. Read the object with readRDS(), then convert it with convertFromPhyloseq().
    3. importMetaPhlAn().
    4. importHUMAnN(). The pathways describe the same samples but different features, so they form a second table. Combining several tables is the topic of the multi-omics lesson.
    Callout

    Learn more

    See the Import chapter of OMA for complete examples with each import function.

    Key Points
    • Choices made during data generation, such as sample storage, DNA extraction and batches, leave a mark on the data. Read how the samples were collected and processed before you analyse them.
    • Pre-processing turns raw reads (FASTQ files) into tables of taxa. It is usually done outside R, before the analysis that this lesson covers.
    • The numbers in the abundance table describe the sequenced DNA, and their total depends on the sequencing depth.
    • The outputs go into the parts of a TreeSE: the abundance table into assay, the taxonomy into rowData, the sample information into colData and the tree into rowTree.
    • mia has import functions, such as importQIIME2(), importMetaPhlAn() and convertFromPhyloseq(), that build a TreeSE directly from pipeline output.

    Content from RStudio project and experimental data

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 25 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I organize my work for this lesson?
    • How do I get the data used in this lesson?

    Objectives

    • Create an RStudio project with a folder for the data.
    • Download the lesson data.
    • Check that the required packages are installed.

    Create an RStudio project

    It is good practice to keep all files of one analysis in one folder. An RStudio project helps with this: when you open the project, R automatically uses the project folder as its working directory. All file paths in this lesson are relative to this folder.

    1. In RStudio, choose File → New Project → New Directory → New Project.
    2. Name the project microbiome-lesson and choose where to save it.
    3. Click Create Project.

    Next, create a folder called data inside the project for the input files. You can use the New Folder button in the Files pane, or run:

    R 

    dir.create("data")

    Finally, open a new R script (File → New File → R Script) and save it in the project folder, for example as microbiome-analysis.R. Write the code of the following episodes into this script, so that you can run it again later.

    Prerequisite

    New to R and RStudio?

    This lesson assumes you know the basics of R and RStudio. If you need a refresher, see the Introduction to data analysis with R and Bioconductor lesson.

    Download the data

    The data consists of the four parts of a microbiome dataset (see episode 1), each in its own file:

    File Content
    taxonomy_abundance.csv Abundance table: taxa × samples
    taxonomy_table.csv Taxonomy of each taxon
    sample_metadata.csv Information about each sample
    phylogeny.tree Phylogenetic tree of the taxa

    We download them into the data folder with download.file(). Here is the first one:

    R 

    download.file(
    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microbiome/microbiome-lesson/main/episodes/data/taxonomy_abundance.csv",
    destfile = file.path("data", "taxonomy_abundance.csv")
)
    Callout

    File paths with file.path()

    The function file.path() joins folder and file names into a path: file.path("data", "taxonomy_abundance.csv") gives "data/taxonomy_abundance.csv". Forward slashes work on Windows, macOS and Linux alike, but file.path() saves you from typing the separators yourself, so we use it for all file paths in this lesson.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Download the other files

    Download the remaining three files (taxonomy_table.csv, sample_metadata.csv and phylogeny.tree) into the data folder. Then check that all four files are there.

    R 

    url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microbiome/microbiome-lesson/main/episodes/data/"

download.file(paste0(url, "taxonomy_table.csv"), file.path("data", "taxonomy_table.csv"))
download.file(paste0(url, "sample_metadata.csv"), file.path("data", "sample_metadata.csv"))
download.file(paste0(url, "phylogeny.tree"), file.path("data", "phylogeny.tree"))

list.files("data")

    Check the packages

    We use these packages:

    Package Used for Episodes
    mia Microbiome analysis all
    miaViz Microbiome visualization all
    ape Reading the phylogenetic tree 4
    scater Principal component analysis (PCA) 7
    bluster Clustering 7, 10
    daa Simple statistical tests (Wilcoxon test, t-test, linear model) 5, 6, 8
    maaslin3 Differential abundance and prevalence 8, 10
    mikropml Machine learning 9

    mia, miaViz and daa belong to the OMA framework. Each episode loads the packages it needs with library().

    If you followed the setup instructions, the packages are already installed. Check that they load without errors:

    R 

    library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(ape)
library(scater)
library(bluster)
library(maaslin3)
library(mikropml)

    We do not load the daa package with library(). Instead, we call its functions with daa:: in front, as in daa::getLm(). Check that it is installed by asking for its version:

    R 

    packageVersion("daa")

    OUTPUT 

    [1] '0.99.0'

    Messages are normal. If you see an error such as there is no package called 'mia', go back to the setup instructions.

    Key Points
    • Use an RStudio project to keep the data, code and results of an analysis together.
    • Use download.file() to download data from the internet, and file.path() to build file paths.
    • The main packages of this lesson are mia and miaViz from the OMA framework; later episodes also use ape, scater, bluster, daa, maaslin3 and mikropml.

    Content from Importing data into TreeSummarizedExperiment

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 75 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do we load microbiome data into R?
    • Why do we store the data in a single object?
    • What is in our study data?

    Objectives

    • Create a TreeSummarizedExperiment object from an abundance table, a taxonomy table, sample information and a tree.
    • Access the abundance table, the taxonomy and the sample information of the object.
    • Select a subset of the samples.
    • Plot how many samples are in each study group.

    Where are we?

    The sequencing reads of our study have already been turned into tables. In this episode, we bring these tables into R and combine them into a single data object. All later steps start from this object.

    Load packages

    R 

    library(mia)
library(miaViz)

    Read the data files

    We start by reading the four files from episode 3 into R. The first column of each CSV file contains the row names, so we use row.names = 1.

    R 

    counts  <- read.csv(file.path("data", "taxonomy_abundance.csv"), row.names = 1)
taxa    <- read.csv(file.path("data", "taxonomy_table.csv"), row.names = 1)
samples <- read.csv(file.path("data", "sample_metadata.csv"), row.names = 1)
tree    <- ape::read.tree(file.path("data", "phylogeny.tree"))

    Let’s take a quick look at each of them. The abundance table has one row per taxon and one column per sample. The row names start with the taxonomic rank of the taxon, such as species-, and the column names are sample IDs:

    R 

    dim(counts)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 308  60

    R 

    counts[1:3, 1:3]

    OUTPUT 

                                          GupDM_A_11 GupDM_A_15 GupDM_A1
species-Escherichia_coli                 1632336    5666898  6814491
species-Alistipes_putredinis              964884          0   225222
species-Porphyromonas_asaccharolytica     463162          0    92810

    The taxonomy table has one row per taxon:

    R 

    head(taxa, n = 3)

    OUTPUT 

                                          superkingdom         phylum
species-Escherichia_coli                  Bacteria Proteobacteria
species-Alistipes_putredinis              Bacteria   Bacteroidota
species-Porphyromonas_asaccharolytica     Bacteria   Bacteroidota
                                                    class            order
species-Escherichia_coli              Gammaproteobacteria Enterobacterales
species-Alistipes_putredinis                  Bacteroidia    Bacteroidales
species-Porphyromonas_asaccharolytica         Bacteroidia    Bacteroidales
                                                  family         genus
species-Escherichia_coli              Enterobacteriaceae   Escherichia
species-Alistipes_putredinis               Rikenellaceae     Alistipes
species-Porphyromonas_asaccharolytica Porphyromonadaceae Porphyromonas
                                                            species
species-Escherichia_coli                           Escherichia coli
species-Alistipes_putredinis                   Alistipes putredinis
species-Porphyromonas_asaccharolytica Porphyromonas asaccharolytica

    The sample information has one row per sample:

    R 

    samples[1:3, c("disease", "age", "gender", "location")]

    OUTPUT 

               disease age gender location
GupDM_A_11     CRC  41 female   Kerala
GupDM_A_15     CRC  59   male   Kerala
GupDM_A1       CRC  62   male   Kerala

    And the tree connects the taxa:

    R 

    tree

    OUTPUT 

    
Phylogenetic tree with 10430 tips and 10429 internal nodes.

Tip labels:
  k__Archaea|p__Candidatus_Micrarchaeota|c__Candidatus_Micrarchaeota_unclassified|o__Candidatus_Micrarchaeota_unclassified|f__Candidatus_Micrarchaeota_unclassified|g__Candidatus_Micrarchaeota_unclassified|s__Candidatus_Micrarchaeota_archaeon_CG1_02_55_22, k__Archaea|p__Archaea_unclassified|c__Archaea_unclassified|o__Archaea_unclassified|f__Archaea_unclassified|g__Archaea_unclassified|s__archaeon_GW2011_AR15, k__Archaea|p__Candidatus_Diapherotrites|c__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_unclassified|o__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_unclassified|f__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_unclassified|g__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_unclassified|s__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_archaeon_CG08_land_8_20_14_0_20_34_12, k__Archaea|p__Archaea_unclassified|c__Archaea_unclassified|o__Archaea_unclassified|f__Archaea_unclassified|g__Archaea_unclassified|s__archaeon_GW2011_AR10, k__Archaea|p__Candidatus_Diapherotrites|c__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_unclassified|o__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_unclassified|f__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_unclassified|g__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_unclassified|s__Candidatus_Diapherotrites_archaeon_CG11_big_fil_rev_8_21_14_0_20_37_9, k__Archaea|p__Euryarchaeota|c__Euryarchaeota_unclassified|o__Euryarchaeota_unclassified|f__Euryarchaeota_unclassified|g__Euryarchaeota_unclassified|s__Euryarchaeota_archaeon_TMED173, ...

Rooted; includes branch length(s).

    The tree is a reference tree from MetaPhlAn, the tool that produced our tables. It contains 10430 species, many more than the 308 in our data. That is fine: each of our taxa has a tip with the same name in the tree, and this is how R knows which tip belongs to which taxon. The printout shows the first few tip labels, which belong to species that are not in our data.

    Why put everything into one object?

    We now have four separate objects that describe the same data. This is risky: if we remove a sample from the abundance table, we have to remember to remove it from the sample information too. If we forget, the tables no longer match, and our results will be wrong without any warning.

    The solution is to store everything in a single object that keeps the parts in sync. In Bioconductor, microbiome data is stored in a TreeSummarizedExperiment (TreeSE for short).

    Figure: the TreeSummarizedExperiment class (Huang et al. 2021, F1000Research). Source: OMA.

    The figure shows all the parts a TreeSE can hold. In this lesson, we only need these four:

    Part Contains In our data
    assays The abundance tables. Rows are taxa, columns are samples. Read counts
    rowData Information about the rows (taxa) Taxonomy
    colData Information about the columns (samples) Disease, age, gender, location, …
    rowTree A tree that connects the rows Phylogenetic tree
    Callout

    TreeSE and SummarizedExperiment

    If you have used the SummarizedExperiment class before, for example in the Introduction to data analysis with R and Bioconductor lesson: a TreeSE is a SummarizedExperiment with extra room for trees. Everything you know about SummarizedExperiment also works for TreeSE. The only difference in our data is what the rows are: genes in that lesson, taxa here. The functions assay(), rowData() and colData() and subsetting with [ , ] work exactly as you learned there.

    Create the TreeSE

    We combine the four parts with the function TreeSummarizedExperiment(). The abundance table must be a matrix, so we convert it with as.matrix(). We also give the data a name with mainExpName. This becomes useful in the bonus section of the next episode, where we store the data at several taxonomic ranks in the same object.

    R 

    tse <- TreeSummarizedExperiment(
    assays  = list(counts = as.matrix(counts)),
    rowData = taxa,
    colData = samples,
    rowTree = tree,
    mainExpName = "main"
)
tse

    OUTPUT

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Where is the information?

    In which part of tse would you find the age of each person?

    1. assay(tse, "counts")
    2. rowData(tse)
    3. colData(tse)
    4. rowTree(tse)
    1. colData(tse). Age describes a sample (a person), and information about samples is stored in colData. You can get the ages with tse$age.
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Which phylum?

    Find out which phylum the first taxon in tse belongs to.

    Hint: the taxonomy is in rowData(tse), and its columns are named superkingdom, phylum, class, …

    R 

    rownames(tse)[1]

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "species-Escherichia_coli"

    R 

    rowData(tse)$phylum[1]

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "Proteobacteria"

    Select a subset of samples

    A TreeSE can be subset with square brackets [rows, columns], just like a data frame. Rows are taxa and columns are samples. To keep only the samples from people with CRC, we select the columns where disease is "CRC":

    R 

    tse_crc <- tse[, tse$disease == "CRC"]
tse_crc

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Healthy people only

    1. Create an object tse_healthy that contains only the samples from healthy people.
    2. How many samples does it have?

    R 

    tse_healthy <- tse[, tse$disease == "healthy"]
ncol(tse_healthy)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 30

    A first look at the study

    Before any analysis, it is good to know who is in the study. The miaViz function plotBarplot() counts the samples in each group of a colData column (col.var):

    R 

    plotBarplot(tse, col.var = "disease")

    Result: the study has 30 people with CRC and 30 healthy people.

    The people come from two places: the city of Bhopal and the state of Kerala. With fill.by, we can colour the bars by a second variable:

    R 

    plotBarplot(tse, col.var = "location", fill.by = "disease")
    Challenge

    Challenge 4: What do you notice?

    Look at the plot above.

    1. From which location do most of the healthy people come?
    2. Suppose we find that the microbiome of CRC patients differs from that of healthy people. Why could this be a problem?
    1. Most healthy people come from Bhopal, while the CRC patients come equally from both places. You can check the numbers with table(tse$location, tse$disease).
    2. Diet and lifestyle differ between the places, and they affect the gut microbiome. A difference between CRC and healthy people could therefore be partly a difference between the two places. We will take this into account in the episodes on beta diversity and differential abundance.

    Save the object

    We save the TreeSE so that we can load it again in the next episode, without repeating the import steps.

    R 

    saveRDS(tse, file.path("data", "tse.rds"))
    Callout

    Importing your own data

    In this lesson, we built the TreeSE from plain tables. Your own data probably comes from a tool such as QIIME 2, MetaPhlAn or mothur, or is stored as a phyloseq object. The mia package has functions that import these formats directly into a TreeSE. See the Import chapter of OMA.

    Key Points
    • A TreeSummarizedExperiment keeps the abundance table, taxonomy, sample information and tree together and in sync.
    • Rows are taxa and columns are samples.
    • assay(), rowData() and colData() access the abundance table, the taxonomy and the sample information.
    • Subsetting with [rows, columns] keeps all parts of the object in sync.
    • plotBarplot() gives a quick overview of the study groups. In our study, the groups differ in more than disease: most healthy people come from Bhopal.

    Content from Exploring and preparing microbiome data

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 130 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How deeply was each sample sequenced?
    • How do we look at the data at a higher taxonomic level, such as phylum?
    • Why and how do we transform the counts?
    • Which bacteria dominate the gut of the people in our study?

    Objectives

    • Plot the library sizes of the samples and explain why they matter.
    • Agglomerate the data to a higher taxonomic rank.
    • Transform counts into relative abundances and robust CLR (rclr) values, and explain what rclr does with the zeros.
    • Plot the community composition of the samples and the abundance of a single taxon.
    • Remove rare taxa with a prevalence filter.
    • (Bonus) Store all taxonomic ranks in one object, and work with one rank using altExp() and swapAltExp().

    Where are we?

    We have our data in a TreeSE. Before we can answer our research question, we need to process the data: check its quality, summarize it and transform it. We also take a first look at which bacteria are in the samples.

    Load packages and data

    R 

    library(mia)
library(miaViz)

    We load the TreeSE that we saved in the previous episode.

    R 

    tse <- readRDS(file.path("data", "tse.rds"))

    Library size

    In episode 1, we learned that the total number of reads per sample, the library size, depends on the sequencing and not on the biology. Let’s check how much it varies. We sum the counts of each sample (column) and store the result as a new column in colData:

    R 

    tse$library_size <- colSums(assay(tse, "counts"))
summary(tse$library_size)

    OUTPUT 

        Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.
 3283981  6947241  8709694  9222329 10478061 27686725

    The miaViz function plotHistogram() shows the distribution. With binwidth, we set the width of each bar, here one million reads:

    R 

    plotHistogram(tse, col.var = "library_size", binwidth = 1e6)

    Result: the largest sample has about 8 times more reads than the smallest. If we compared raw counts, the samples with more reads would seem to have more of everything. We fix this with a transformation below.

    Agglomeration: moving up the tree of life

    Our data is at the species level. Sometimes it is easier to look at bigger groups, such as genera or phyla. Combining all taxa that belong to the same group is called agglomeration. The counts of the taxa in a group are summed.

    R 

    tse_phylum <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "phylum")
rownames(tse_phylum)

    OUTPUT 

     [1] "Actinobacteria"             "Bacteroidota"
 [3] "Candidatus Melainabacteria" "Euryarchaeota"
 [5] "Firmicutes"                 "Fusobacteria"
 [7] "Lentisphaerae"              "Proteobacteria"
 [9] "Spirochaetes"               "Synergistetes"
[11] "Verrucomicrobia"

    Result: the 308 species belong to 11 phyla.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: How many genera?

    1. Agglomerate the data to the genus level and save the result as tse_genus.
    2. How many genera are in the data?

    R 

    tse_genus <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "genus")
nrow(tse_genus)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 104

    Relative abundance

    To compare samples with different library sizes, we transform the counts. The simplest transformation is the relative abundance: each count is divided by the library size of its sample. The result is the share of each taxon in the sample. For example, a taxon with 500 reads in a sample of 1000 reads has a relative abundance of 0.5 (50 %).

    The function transformAssay() adds a transformed table to the TreeSE:

    R 

    tse <- transformAssay(tse, assay.type = "counts", method = "relabundance")
assayNames(tse)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "counts"       "relabundance"

    The TreeSE now holds two tables: the original counts and the new relabundance table. The original counts are kept.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Relative abundances

    1. What do you expect the relative abundances of each sample (column) to sum to?
    2. Check your answer for the first five samples.

    Hint: colSums() sums the columns of a table.

    1. They sum to 1, because each value is the share of one taxon in the sample.
    2. Check with colSums():

    R 

    colSums(assay(tse, "relabundance"))[1:5]

    OUTPUT 

    GupDM_A_11 GupDM_A_15   GupDM_A1  GupDM_A10  GupDM_A12
         1          1          1          1          1

    Community composition

    Which bacteria dominate the gut of the people in our study? The miaViz function plotAbundance() draws a stacked bar for each sample. With group = "phylum", the taxa are agglomerated to phyla for the plot, and col.var = "disease" together with facet.cols = TRUE splits the samples into one panel per disease group. scales = "free_x" lets each panel show only its own samples.

    R 

    plotAbundance(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance", group = "phylum",
    col.var = "disease", facet.cols = TRUE, scales = "free_x"
)

    WARNING 

    Warning: Removed 355 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_bar()`).

    Result: each bar is one person. Bacteroidota dominate most samples in both groups, followed by Firmicutes, but the communities vary a lot between people. Our eyes cannot tell from this plot whether the two groups differ. The analyses in the next episodes can.

    plotAbundance() may print a warning such as Removed 355 rows containing missing values. It is harmless: the plot does not draw bars for taxa with zero abundance.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: The most abundant genera

    Which five genera are the most abundant in the data?

    Hint: use tse_genus from challenge 1 and the function getTop().

    R 

    getTop(tse_genus, top = 5)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "Prevotella"      "Bacteroides"     "Phocaeicola"     "Escherichia"
[5] "Bifidobacterium"

    getTop() ranks the taxa by their mean abundance across the samples (by default in the counts table). Prevotella is the most abundant genus.

    A closer look at one species

    The most abundant species in the data is Prevotella copri. The miaViz function plotBoxplot() shows its relative abundance in each group. With features, we choose the taxon to plot, and with x, the groups:

    R 

    plotBoxplot(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance",
    features = "species-Prevotella_copri", x = "disease"
)

    Result: in healthy people, P. copri makes up a median of 47 % of the whole community, compared to 1 % in people with CRC. A single species dominates the gut of many healthy people in this study. Keep this species in mind: we will meet it again in every episode that follows.

    Robust CLR transformation

    Relative abundances are intuitive, but they have a catch that we met in episode 1: because the shares of a sample always sum to 1, an increase of one taxon makes all the others look smaller. Log-ratio transformations are designed for this kind of relative (compositional) data. A ratio compares two taxa in the same sample, so it does not change when the sample is sequenced more deeply. The logarithm makes the ratios symmetric: a taxon that is twice as abundant as another gets log(2) = 0.69, and one that is half as abundant gets log(1/2) = -0.69.

    The centred log-ratio (CLR) compares each taxon to the “average” taxon of the same sample (the geometric mean), on a log scale:

    • a positive value means that the taxon is more abundant than average in that sample;
    • a negative value means that it is less abundant than average;
    • zero means that it is exactly average.

    The logarithm of zero is not defined, and 84 % of our table is zeros. The robust CLR (rclr) solves this in two steps. First, it calculates the average from the non-zero values only. Then it fills in the zeros with estimates based on the main patterns in the whole table (matrix completion). In the version we use, all values are replaced by these smoothed estimates. The rclr values therefore describe the broad patterns in the data well, but a single value is an estimate, not a measurement. This is why we use rclr for methods that look at the whole table, such as PCA in episode 7, and relative abundances to plot single taxa.

    R 

    tse <- transformAssay(tse, assay.type = "counts", method = "rclr")
assayNames(tse)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "counts"       "relabundance" "rclr"

    The TreeSE now holds three tables: counts, relabundance and rclr.

    Why transform at all? Many statistical methods, such as PCA and the t-test, work best when the values are roughly normally distributed. Let’s compare the distribution of all values in the counts and rclr tables:

    R 

    plotHistogram(tse, assay.type = "counts", binwidth = 1e5)

    R 

    plotHistogram(tse, assay.type = "rclr", binwidth = 0.25)

    Result: the counts are mostly zeros with a long tail of very large values. The rclr values form a bell-shaped distribution around zero, which suits many statistical methods much better.

    Challenge

    Challenge 4: What happened to the zeros?

    Compare the counts and the rclr values of the first three taxa in the first three samples:

    R 

    assay(tse, "counts")[1:3, 1:3]

    OUTPUT 

                                          GupDM_A_11 GupDM_A_15 GupDM_A1
species-Escherichia_coli                 1632336    5666898  6814491
species-Alistipes_putredinis              964884          0   225222
species-Porphyromonas_asaccharolytica     463162          0    92810

    R 

    assay(tse, "rclr")[1:3, 1:3]

    OUTPUT 

                                          GupDM_A_11 GupDM_A_15 GupDM_A1
species-Escherichia_coli               1.0405323  1.7524587 4.724694
species-Alistipes_putredinis           0.6682048  1.3053407 2.961278
species-Porphyromonas_asaccharolytica  0.2550027  0.4543376 1.192139
    1. Is Escherichia coli more or less abundant than the average taxon in the first sample?
    2. In the second sample, two taxa have a count of zero. Which rclr values did they get? Were these taxa measured in that sample?
    1. Its rclr value is 1.04. It is positive, so E. coli is more abundant than the average taxon in that sample.
    2. They got the values 1.31 and 0.45, although the taxa were not detected in that sample. The rclr filled in the zeros with estimates based on the patterns in the whole table. Keep in mind that these values are estimates, not measurements.

    Removing rare taxa

    Many taxa are found in only a few samples. The share of samples in which a taxon is found is called its prevalence. For some analyses, such as differential abundance in episode 8, it is useful to remove rare taxa: they carry little information and add many tests.

    The function subsetByPrevalent() keeps only taxa that are found in at least a given share of the samples. Here, a taxon must have a relative abundance of at least 0.1 % (detection = 0.001) in at least 10 % of the samples (prevalence = 0.1):

    R 

    tse_prevalent <- subsetByPrevalent(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance",
    detection = 0.001, prevalence = 0.1
)
dim(tse_prevalent)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 94 60

    Result: only 94 of the 308 species remain.

    Callout

    Filter or not?

    Rare taxa are part of the diversity of a community. For the diversity analyses in episodes 6 and 7, we therefore use all taxa. We use the filtered data only for differential abundance analysis in episode 8.

    Challenge

    Challenge 5: A stricter filter

    1. How many species remain if a species must be found in at least 50 % of the samples?
    2. What does this tell you about the gut microbiomes of the people in this study?

    R 

    tse_prevalent50 <- subsetByPrevalent(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance",
    detection = 0.001, prevalence = 0.5
)
nrow(tse_prevalent50)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 13
    1. Only 13 species are found in at least half of the people.
    2. Most species are found in only a few people: every gut microbiome is different.

    Save the object

    We save the TreeSE, which now contains the library sizes and the transformed tables, for the next episodes.

    R 

    saveRDS(tse, file.path("data", "tse_processed.rds"))
    Callout

    Which table for which analysis?

    There is no fixed rule: the right table depends on the method and on its assumptions. Some common choices:

    • Alpha diversity is usually calculated from counts or relative abundances.
    • Composition plots and Bray–Curtis dissimilarity use relative abundances.
    • PCA and other methods that expect roughly normal values use rclr (or CLR) values.
    • Differential abundance methods differ: some use log-transformed relative abundances (as we do in episode 8), some CLR values, and some model the counts directly.

    Always check what the method you use expects. Many more transformations are available; see the Transformation chapter of OMA.

    Challenge

    Challenge 6: Explore the data at family level (30 minutes)

    In this exercise, you use what you learned in this episode to explore the data at the family level.

    1. Check that the library sizes do not differ between the disease groups: plot library_size by disease with plotBoxplot() and test the difference with the Wilcoxon test, daa::getWilcoxonTest(tse, library_size ~ disease) (we explain this test in the next episode). Why is it good news if they do not differ?
    2. Agglomerate the data to the family level with agglomerateByRank(), and add relative abundances with transformAssay().
    3. Find the five most abundant families with getTop() (use the relabundance table).
    4. Plot the relative abundance of these five families by disease with plotBoxplot().
    5. Which family dominates the healthy samples? Which family is more abundant in CRC? Write two sentences on how this fits with what you learned about Prevotella copri.

    1. Library size

    R 

    plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "library_size", x = "disease")

    R 

    library_test <- daa::getWilcoxonTest(tse, library_size ~ disease)
library_test

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 1 × 8
  rownames     .y.          group1 group2     n1    n2 statistic     p
* <chr>        <chr>        <chr>  <chr>   <int> <int>     <dbl> <dbl>
1 library_size library_size CRC    healthy    30    30       438 0.866

    The library sizes do not differ between the groups (p = 0.87). This is good news: if one group had been sequenced much more deeply, differences between the groups could partly be caused by the sequencing.

    2.–4. Family level

    R 

    tse_family <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "family")

    WARNING 

    Warning: 'rclr' includes negative values.
Agglomeration of it might lead to meaningless values.
Check the assay, and consider doing transformation againmanually with agglomerated data.

    R 

    tse_family <- transformAssay(
    tse_family, assay.type = "counts", method = "relabundance"
)
top_families <- getTop(tse_family, top = 5, assay.type = "relabundance")
top_families

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "Prevotellaceae"     "Bacteroidaceae"     "Enterobacteriaceae"
[4] "Lachnospiraceae"    "Oscillospiraceae"

    R 

    plotBoxplot(
    tse_family, assay.type = "relabundance", x = "disease",
    features = top_families, facet.by = "rownames"
)

    agglomerateByRank() warns that 'rclr' includes negative values. Agglomeration sums the values of all tables. Summed counts are fine, but summed rclr values are meaningless. The rule is: agglomerate first, then transform. This is why we calculated the relative abundances again after agglomerating.

    5. Prevotellaceae dominate the healthy samples (median 63 % vs 32 % in CRC), while Bacteroidaceae are more abundant in CRC (median 18 % vs 2 %). Most of the Prevotellaceae in healthy people is Prevotella copri; in CRC, its place is partly taken by Bacteroides.

    Bonus: all ranks in one object

    This section is optional. It shows a way to keep the data at all taxonomic ranks in one object, which is handy in larger analyses. The next episodes do not need it.

    So far, we created a separate object for each rank (tse_phylum, tse_genus, tse_family). With many ranks, this quickly becomes hard to manage: each object must be transformed, subset and saved on its own.

    Instead, we can keep all ranks in one object. The function agglomerateByRanks() agglomerates the data to every taxonomic rank at once:

    R 

    tse <- agglomerateByRanks(tse)
altExpNames(tse)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "superkingdom" "phylum"       "class"        "order"        "family"
[6] "genus"        "species"

    When you run this, R prints a warning for each rank (we hide them on this page): 'rclr' includes negative values. Agglomeration sums the values of all tables. Summed counts are fine, but summed rclr values are meaningless. The rule is: agglomerate first, then transform. We therefore transform the agglomerated data again below.

    The main data is still the species-level data that we named "main" in episode 4. Each rank is stored inside the TreeSE as an alternative experiment (altExp): a complete TreeSE of its own, with the same samples. We pick one with altExp():

    R 

    altExp(tse, "phylum")

    OUTPUT 

    class: TreeSummarizedExperiment
dim: 11 60
metadata(1): agglomerated_by_rank
assays(3): counts relabundance rclr
rownames(11): Actinobacteria Bacteroidota ... Synergistetes
  Verrucomicrobia
rowData names(7): superkingdom phylum ... genus species
colnames(60): GupDM_A_11 GupDM_A_15 ... GupDM_JO GupDM_JP
colData names(28): study_name subject_id ... disease_location
  library_size
reducedDimNames(0):
mainExpName: main
altExpNames(0):
rowLinks: a LinkDataFrame (11 rows)
rowTree: 1 phylo tree(s) (11 leaves)
colLinks: NULL
colTree: NULL

    With the altexp argument, transformAssay() transforms the main data and all the alternative experiments with a single command:

    R 

    tse <- transformAssay(
    tse, assay.type = "counts", method = "relabundance",
    altexp = altExpNames(tse)
)
tse <- transformAssay(
    tse, assay.type = "counts", method = "rclr",
    altexp = altExpNames(tse)
)
assayNames(altExp(tse, "phylum"))

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "counts"       "relabundance" "rclr"

    The table names are the same as before, but the meaningless summed relabundance and rclr tables have now been replaced by tables calculated from the agglomerated counts.

    Most functions work on the main data of a TreeSE. To analyse another rank, we make it the main data with swapAltExp(). The family-level data already has the sample information, so withColData = FALSE tells the function not to copy it a second time from the old main data:

    R 

    tse_family <- swapAltExp(tse, "family", withColData = FALSE)
tse_family

    OUTPUT 

    class: TreeSummarizedExperiment
dim: 48 60
metadata(1): agglomerated_by_rank
assays(3): counts relabundance rclr
rownames(48): Acidaminococcaceae Actinomycetaceae ... Veillonellaceae
  Victivallaceae
rowData names(7): superkingdom phylum ... genus species
colnames(60): GupDM_A_11 GupDM_A_15 ... GupDM_JO GupDM_JP
colData names(28): study_name subject_id ... disease_location
  library_size
reducedDimNames(0):
mainExpName: family
altExpNames(7): superkingdom phylum ... species main
rowLinks: a LinkDataFrame (48 rows)
rowTree: 1 phylo tree(s) (48 leaves)
colLinks: NULL
colTree: NULL

    tse_family has families as its rows (mainExpName: family), and its other ranks, including the original "main" data, are still available as alternative experiments.

    Callout

    Why alternative experiments?

    Alternative experiments are harder to understand than separate objects, but they have big advantages: all ranks share the same sample information, they stay in sync when we subset samples, one command transforms all of them, and we save a single object.

    Challenge

    Challenge 7 (bonus): Working at the genus level

    1. Use swapAltExp() to make the genus level the main data. Store the result in tse_genus.
    2. Which tables (assays) does it have?
    3. Find the five most abundant genera with getTop(). Do you get the same answer as in challenge 3?

    R 

    tse_genus <- swapAltExp(tse, "genus", withColData = FALSE)
assayNames(tse_genus)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "counts"       "relabundance" "rclr"

    R 

    getTop(tse_genus, top = 5)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "Prevotella"      "Bacteroides"     "Phocaeicola"     "Escherichia"
[5] "Bifidobacterium"

    The genus-level data already has the relabundance and rclr tables, and the top genera are the same as in challenge 3.

    Key Points
    • Library sizes differ between samples, so we compare relative values instead of raw counts.
    • agglomerateByRank() combines taxa into a higher taxonomic rank.
    • (Bonus) agglomerateByRanks() stores the data at every rank as alternative experiments in one object; altExp() picks one, and swapAltExp() makes one the main data.
    • transformAssay() adds transformed tables, such as relative abundance and robust CLR (rclr), and keeps the original counts.
    • rclr compares each taxon to the average taxon of its sample on a log scale. It fills in the zeros with estimates, so single rclr values are estimates, not measurements.
    • Which table to use depends on the method and its assumptions. The rclr values are closer to a normal distribution than the counts.
    • plotAbundance() shows the community composition of each sample, and plotBoxplot() the abundance of a single taxon by group.
    • subsetByPrevalent() removes rare taxa. Use it for differential abundance, but not for diversity.
    • In our study, one species, Prevotella copri, dominates the gut of many healthy people.

    Content from Alpha diversity

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 105 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is alpha diversity?
    • How do we calculate alpha diversity?
    • Does alpha diversity differ between people with colorectal cancer and healthy people?

    Objectives

    • Explain the difference between richness, evenness and diversity.
    • Calculate alpha diversity indices with addAlpha().
    • Plot alpha diversity by study group.
    • Test whether alpha diversity differs between two groups with the Wilcoxon test, and interpret the result.

    Where are we?

    Our data is imported and processed. Now we start the statistical analysis that answers our research question. The first question is: do people with CRC and healthy people differ in the diversity of their gut microbiome?

    Load packages and data

    R 

    library(mia)
library(miaViz)

    R 

    tse <- readRDS(file.path("data", "tse_processed.rds"))

    What is alpha diversity?

    Alpha diversity describes the diversity within one sample. Imagine two gardens with the same ten kinds of flowers:

    • In garden A, all ten kinds are equally common.
    • In garden B, one kind makes up 91 % of all flowers, and the other nine are rare.

    In the picture below, each point is one flower and each colour is one kind:

    Both gardens have the same number of flower kinds, but garden A feels more diverse. Alpha diversity captures this with different measures, called indices:

    Index Question it answers Values
    Richness (observed richness) How many different taxa are there? The number of taxa
    Evenness (Pielou’s evenness) Are the taxa equally common, or do a few dominate? From 0 (one taxon dominates) to 1 (all equally common)
    Diversity (Shannon index) Combines richness and evenness into one number. From 0 upwards; typically 1–5 in gut samples
    Phylogenetic diversity (Faith’s index) How much of the tree of life do the taxa cover? The total branch length of the tree

    For all indices, a higher value means a more diverse sample.

    These indices give complementary information. Two samples can have the same richness but a different evenness, as in the gardens above, or the same Shannon diversity for different reasons. Phylogenetic diversity adds whether the taxa are close relatives or come from distant branches of the tree. It is therefore good practice to look at several indices, not only one.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: What does alpha diversity measure?

    1. The diversity between different habitats
    2. The diversity within a single community or habitat
    3. The total number of ecosystems in a region
    1. The diversity within a single community or habitat. The differences between communities are called beta diversity, the topic of the next episode.
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Two gardens

    Look at gardens A and B in the figure above.

    1. Which garden has the higher richness?
    2. Which garden has the higher evenness?
    3. Which garden has the higher Shannon diversity?
    1. Neither: both have ten kinds of flowers, so the richness is the same.
    2. Garden A, because all kinds are equally common.
    3. Garden A. Shannon diversity combines richness and evenness, and garden A has the same richness but a higher evenness.

    Calculate alpha diversity

    The function addAlpha() calculates alpha diversity indices from the counts. The transformations of the previous episode are not needed here. We choose the indices with the index argument:

    R 

    tse <- addAlpha(
    tse, assay.type = "counts",
    index = c(
        "observed_richness", "pielou_evenness",
        "shannon_diversity", "faith_diversity"
    )
)

    The results are added as new columns to colData, next to the other sample information:

    R 

    colData(tse)[, c(
    "disease", "observed_richness", "pielou_evenness",
    "shannon_diversity", "faith_diversity"
)]

    OUTPUT 

    DataFrame with 60 rows and 5 columns
               disease observed_richness pielou_evenness shannon_diversity
           <character>         <numeric>       <numeric>         <numeric>
GupDM_A_11         CRC                55        0.687513           2.75509
GupDM_A_15         CRC                29        0.310196           1.04452
GupDM_A1           CRC               149        0.665661           3.33093
GupDM_A10          CRC                69        0.653870           2.76856
GupDM_A12          CRC                64        0.633120           2.63307
...                ...               ...             ...               ...
GupDM_JL           CRC                46        0.684066           2.61904
GupDM_JM           CRC                70        0.682164           2.89817
GupDM_JN           CRC                71        0.685038           2.92010
GupDM_JO           CRC                89        0.696916           3.12820
GupDM_JP           CRC                86        0.778372           3.46714
           faith_diversity
                 <numeric>
GupDM_A_11         8.49226
GupDM_A_15         5.49297
GupDM_A1          17.55391
GupDM_A10          9.41595
GupDM_A12          9.41699
...                    ...
GupDM_JL           8.90981
GupDM_JM          11.20033
GupDM_JN          11.08878
GupDM_JO          13.03100
GupDM_JP          13.87034

    Faith’s index needs the phylogenetic tree, which addAlpha() finds in the rowTree of the TreeSE.

    Plot alpha diversity

    The miaViz function plotBoxplot() shows the values of a colData column (col.var) for each group (x):

    R 

    plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "shannon_diversity", x = "disease")

    Each point is one person. The Shannon diversity appears higher in the CRC group. But is the difference larger than we would expect by chance?

    Compare the groups with a statistical test

    To compare two groups, we use the Wilcoxon test (also called the Mann–Whitney test). It sorts all values from smallest to largest and checks whether the values of one group tend to rank higher than those of the other. Because it uses only the order of the values, it does not assume that they follow a normal distribution, and a few extreme values do not distort it. This makes it a safe choice for diversity indices, which are often skewed. For more than two groups, the Kruskal–Wallis test (kruskal.test()) works in the same way.

    The test gives a p-value: the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if the two groups did not really differ. In this lesson, we call a result significant when p < 0.05.

    We run the test with daa::getWilcoxonTest() from the daa package. As explained in the setup episode, we write daa:: in front of its functions instead of loading the package. The formula reads “Shannon diversity by disease group”. The left side can be a column of colData, as here, or an assay, as we will see in the differential abundance episode.

    R 

    shannon_test <- daa::getWilcoxonTest(tse, shannon_diversity ~ disease)
shannon_test

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 1 × 8
  rownames          .y.              group1 group2    n1    n2 statistic       p
* <chr>             <chr>            <chr>  <chr>  <int> <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 shannon_diversity shannon_diversi… CRC    healt…    30    30       747 4.11e-6

    Result: the median Shannon diversity is 2.71 in people with CRC and 1.95 in healthy people. The p-value is 4.1e-06, so the difference is very unlikely to be due to chance. People with CRC have a higher Shannon diversity than healthy people.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Richness

    1. Plot the observed richness by disease group.
    2. Test whether the richness differs between the groups.
    3. Which group has more species?

    R 

    plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "observed_richness", x = "disease")

    R 

    richness_test <- daa::getWilcoxonTest(tse, observed_richness ~ disease)
richness_test

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 1 × 8
  rownames          .y.              group1 group2    n1    n2 statistic       p
* <chr>             <chr>            <chr>  <chr>  <int> <int>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 observed_richness observed_richne… CRC    healt…    30    30      700. 1.35e-4

    People with CRC have more species in their gut sample than healthy people (p = 0.00014).

    Is higher diversity healthier?

    A more diverse gut microbiome is often described as a healthy one. Why, then, is diversity lower in the healthy people of our study? Evenness gives a clue.

    Challenge

    Challenge 4: Evenness

    1. Plot Pielou’s evenness by disease group. Which group is less even?
    2. Think back to the previous episode: which species makes up about half of the community in many healthy people?
    3. Use your answers to explain why healthy people have a lower Shannon diversity.

    R 

    plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "pielou_evenness", x = "disease")
    1. Healthy samples are less even.
    2. Prevotella copri.
    3. When one species takes up a large part of the community, the community is uneven, like garden B. A low evenness gives a low Shannon diversity.

    So “higher diversity” does not automatically mean “healthier”. Diet, geography and lifestyle shape the gut microbiome, and Prevotella-dominated guts are common in many non-Western populations. Always interpret diversity in the context of the study.

    Result: the median evenness is 0.54 in healthy people and 0.68 in people with CRC (p = 5.4e-05). The lower Shannon diversity of healthy people is largely due to their lower evenness: in many of them, one species dominates. Richness is higher in CRC too, so evenness is not the whole story. We will see in the next episodes which taxa differ between the groups.

    Challenge

    Challenge 5: Phylogenetic diversity

    1. Does Faith’s phylogenetic diversity differ between the groups? Plot it and run the test.
    2. Which part of the TreeSE does this index use that the other indices do not?

    R 

    plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "faith_diversity", x = "disease")

    R 

    faith_test <- daa::getWilcoxonTest(tse, faith_diversity ~ disease)
faith_test

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 1 × 8
  rownames        .y.             group1 group2     n1    n2 statistic        p
* <chr>           <chr>           <chr>  <chr>   <int> <int>     <dbl>    <dbl>
1 faith_diversity faith_diversity CRC    healthy    30    30       679 0.000543
    1. Yes, it is higher in CRC (p = 0.00054).
    2. The phylogenetic tree (rowTree). Faith’s index measures the total branch length of the tree covered by the taxa in a sample.
    Callout

    Sequencing depth and rarefaction

    The deeper a sample is sequenced, the more rare taxa we find, so richness partly depends on the library size. This is often checked with rarefaction curves, or by randomly subsampling all samples to the same number of reads (rarefying). This applies to both amplicon and shotgun data; addAlpha() can rarefy with its sample and niter arguments.

    Rarefying throws data away, and whether to do it is debated. A simple first check is whether richness is related to the library size. In our data, it is not clearly related (Spearman correlation rho = 0.16, p = 0.23), and the library sizes do not differ between the groups (p = 0.87), so we do not rarefy here. See the Alpha diversity chapter of OMA.

    Challenge

    Challenge 6: Diversity, age and gender (30 minutes)

    Disease is not the only thing we know about the people in our study. Is diversity also related to their age or gender?

    1. Does the Shannon diversity differ between women and men? Make the plot and run the test.
    2. Is the Shannon diversity related to age? Use a correlation test: cor.test(tse$age, tse$shannon_diversity, method = "spearman").
    3. Plot the age of the people by disease group. What do you notice?
    4. Repeat the correlation test separately for the CRC patients and for the healthy people. Is diversity still related to age? Hint: subset the TreeSE to one group, as for any SummarizedExperiment: tse[, tse$disease == "CRC"].
    5. Make age groups with tse$age_group <- cut(tse$age, breaks = c(0, 40, 60, 100), labels = c("under 40", "40-60", "over 60")) and plot the Shannon diversity by age group, coloured by disease (fill.by = "disease").
    6. Write two or three sentences: is diversity related to age in this study?

    1. Gender

    R 

    plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "shannon_diversity", x = "gender")

    R 

    gender_test <- daa::getWilcoxonTest(tse, shannon_diversity ~ gender)
gender_test

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 1 × 8
  rownames          .y.               group1 group2    n1    n2 statistic     p
* <chr>             <chr>             <chr>  <chr>  <int> <int>     <dbl> <dbl>
1 shannon_diversity shannon_diversity female male      30    30       346 0.127

    There is no clear difference between women and men (p = 0.13).

    2. Age

    R 

    age_test <- cor.test(
    tse$age, tse$shannon_diversity, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE
)
age_test

    OUTPUT

S = 24173, p-value = 0.01043

0.328331

    Older people seem to have a higher diversity (rho = 0.33, p = 0.01).

    3. Age by disease

    R 

    plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "age", x = "disease")

    The CRC patients are much older (median 59 years) than the healthy people (median 40 years).

    4. Within each group

    R 

    tse_crc <- tse[, tse$disease == "CRC"]
age_test_crc <- cor.test(
    tse_crc$age, tse_crc$shannon_diversity, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE
