19                         species-_rectale -2.209343     0.016605080

    The prevalence model is a logistic regression: it models whether the taxon is present or absent. Its coef is the change in the log-odds of the taxon being present. The odds are the number of people who carry the taxon divided by the number who do not: 15 carriers and 15 non-carriers give odds of 1, 3 carriers and 27 non-carriers give odds of 1/9. You do not need to interpret the exact value. A positive value means that the taxon is found more often in CRC, and a negative value that it is found less often in CRC.

    Result: 29 species differ in prevalence, of which 21 are found more often in CRC. Only 3 of them also differ in abundance. The prevalence model finds many results that the abundance model misses.

    One of the prevalence results is Flavonifractor plautii. This is the bacterium that the authors of our study highlighted in the title of their paper. getPrevalence() gives the share of samples in which it is present, in each group:

    R 

    getPrevalence(tse[, tse$disease == "CRC"], assay.type = "counts")["species-Flavonifractor_plautii"]

    OUTPUT 

    species-Flavonifractor_plautii
                     0.7333333

    R 

    getPrevalence(tse[, tse$disease == "healthy"], assay.type = "counts")["species-Flavonifractor_plautii"]

    OUTPUT 

    species-Flavonifractor_plautii
                     0.1333333

    R 

    plotBoxplot(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance", x = "disease",
    features = "species-Flavonifractor_plautii"
)

    Result: F. plautii is present in 73 % of the CRC patients but in only 13 % of the healthy people. Its abundance is low in both groups: the clear difference is whether it is there.

    Challenge

    Challenge 4: Bacteroides fragilis

    Some strains of Bacteroides fragilis produce a toxin that has been linked to CRC.

    1. Find species-Bacteroides_fragilis in the prevalence results. What are its coef and qval_individual?
    2. In what share of the CRC patients and of the healthy people is it present?
    3. Does the sign of its coef agree with these shares?

    R 

    res_prevalence[
    res_prevalence$feature == "species-Bacteroides_fragilis",
    c("feature", "coef", "qval_individual")
]

    OUTPUT 

                           feature     coef qval_individual
2 species-Bacteroides_fragilis 2.456524     0.004484035

    R 

    getPrevalence(tse[, tse$disease == "CRC"], assay.type = "counts")["species-Bacteroides_fragilis"]

    OUTPUT 

    species-Bacteroides_fragilis
                         0.8

    R 

    getPrevalence(tse[, tse$disease == "healthy"], assay.type = "counts")["species-Bacteroides_fragilis"]

    OUTPUT 

    species-Bacteroides_fragilis
                   0.2333333

    B. fragilis is present in more CRC patients than healthy people. Its coef is positive, which means “present more often in CRC”, so the sign agrees with the shares.

    Challenge

    Challenge 5 (optional): A famous CRC bacterium

    Fusobacterium nucleatum is one of the bacteria most strongly linked to CRC in the literature, yet it is not in our results. Find out why.

    Hint: load the unfiltered data from data/tse_processed.rds and calculate the prevalence of species-Fusobacterium_nucleatum with getPrevalence().

    R 

    tse_all <- readRDS(file.path("data", "tse_processed.rds"))
prevalence <- getPrevalence(tse_all, assay.type = "counts")
prevalence["species-Fusobacterium_nucleatum"]

    OUTPUT 

    species-Fusobacterium_nucleatum
                     0.06666667

    F. nucleatum was detected in only 7 % of the people, so our prevalence filter (at least 10 % of samples) removed it before the analysis. Filtering always involves a trade-off: it makes the analysis more robust, but it can remove taxa that are rare but interesting.

    Challenge

    Challenge 6: How robust are the results? (30 minutes)

    Our results depend on choices we made: the variables in the formula and the taxonomic rank. In this exercise, you test how robust they are.

    The CRC patients in our study are older than the healthy people (median age 59 vs 40 years), and age also affects the gut microbiome.

    1. Plot age by disease with plotBoxplot(). Are there CRC patients under 40?
    2. Run MaAsLin 3 with formula = ~ disease + location + age (output folder maaslin3_output_age). How many species differ in abundance by disease (q < 0.05)? Are any species associated with age itself?
    3. Now repeat the analysis with ~ disease + location at the genus level (output folder maaslin3_output_genus). Load the full data again, agglomerate it with agglomerateByRank(), and prepare it as at the start of this episode. How many genera differ in abundance?
    4. Is the genus Prevotella significant? Compare with the species-level result for Prevotella copri.
    5. Write two or three sentences: which findings are robust to these choices, and which are not?

    1. Age by disease

    R 

    plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "age", x = "disease")

    R 

    min(tse$age[tse$disease == "CRC"])

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 41

    All CRC patients are at least 41 years old, while many healthy people are younger.

    2. MaAsLin 3 with age

    R 

    fit_age <- maaslin3(
    tse,
    formula = ~ disease + location + age,
    output = "maaslin3_output_age",
    plot_summary_plot = FALSE,
    plot_associations = FALSE,
    verbosity = "ERROR"
)
res_age <- fit_age$fit_data_abundance$results
res_age <- res_age[res_age$qval_individual < 0.05 & !is.na(res_age$qval_individual), ]

sig_age_disease <- res_age[res_age$metadata == "disease", ]
sig_age_disease[, c("feature", "coef", "qval_individual")]

    OUTPUT 

                                   feature      coef qval_individual
1             species-Prevotella_copri -4.270148    0.0002874643
3 species-Faecalibacterium_prausnitzii -2.512047    0.0441288103

    R 

    sum(res_age$metadata == "age")

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 0

    With age in the formula, 2 species differ by disease (11 without age), and 0 species are associated with age. Age and disease are strongly linked in this study, so when both are in the model, it is hard to tell which of them explains a difference. The uncertainty of the disease effect grows and fewer results pass the threshold. To separate the effects of age and disease, we would need a study design in which the groups have similar ages (for example, age-matched controls).

    3. and 4. Genus level

    R 

    tse_genus <- readRDS(file.path("data", "tse_processed.rds"))
tse_genus <- agglomerateByRank(tse_genus, rank = "genus")
tse_genus$disease <- factor(tse_genus$disease, levels = c("healthy", "CRC"))
tse_genus <- transformAssay(
    tse_genus, assay.type = "counts", method = "relabundance"
)
tse_genus <- subsetByPrevalent(
    tse_genus, assay.type = "relabundance",
    detection = 0.001, prevalence = 0.1
)

fit_genus <- maaslin3(
    tse_genus,
    formula = ~ disease + location,
    output = "maaslin3_output_genus",
    plot_summary_plot = FALSE,
    plot_associations = FALSE,
    verbosity = "ERROR"
)
res_genus <- fit_genus$fit_data_abundance$results
res_genus <- res_genus[res_genus$metadata == "disease", ]
sum(res_genus$qval_individual < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 7

    R 

    res_genus[res_genus$feature == "Prevotella", c("feature", "coef", "qval_individual")]

    OUTPUT 

          feature      coef qval_individual
12 Prevotella -1.388461      0.05567889

    At the genus level, 7 genera differ in abundance. The genus Prevotella is not significant (q = 0.056), although Prevotella copri was the strongest species-level result. The genus also contains other Prevotella species, and some of them, such as Prevotella sp. CAG-520, tend to be more abundant in CRC. Summing them with P. copri blurs the difference.

    5. Conclusion

    Results that hold across formulas and ranks are the most robust, for example the lower abundance of Prevotella copri and of the butyrate producer Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in CRC, which remain significant when age is added. Other results change when age is added or when we move to the genus level. The rank you analyse changes the question: “which species?” and “which genera?” are not the same question.

    Key Points
    • Differential abundance analysis tests whether the differences we see in plots are statistically significant.
    • At its core, DAA is a simple test: a t-test is a linear model with one two-group variable, and a linear model can add covariates, such as the location. Most DAA methods are based on this under the hood.
    • Testing many taxa produces false positives, so we use q-values that are corrected for multiple testing.
    • Dedicated methods, such as MaAsLin 3, extend the linear model to take the specific nature of microbiome data into account: relative values, many zeros and noisy abundances.
    • A taxon can differ in abundance, in prevalence (how often it is present), or both. MaAsLin 3 tests both.
    • Look at the data behind the results, and treat significant taxa as candidates for further study.
    • In our study, Prevotella copri and butyrate-producing species are less abundant in people with CRC, and Flavonifractor plautii is found much more often in CRC.

    Content from Machine learning: predicting an outcome

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 95 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How well can we predict an outcome, such as colorectal cancer, from the gut microbiome?
    • Why do we split the data into training and test data?
    • Which bacteria are the most important for the prediction?

    Objectives

    • Explain the terms feature, outcome, training data, test data, overfitting, cross-validation and AUC.
    • Train a random forest model with mikropml to predict an outcome (here, the disease) from the abundance table.
    • Evaluate a model with the cross-validation AUC and the test AUC, and explain why a single small test set is unreliable.
    • Find the most important taxa of a model and compare them with the differential abundance results.

    Where are we?

    We are still in the statistical analysis step. In the beta diversity episode, the samples of people with CRC and healthy people largely separated in the ordination plots, and in the last episode we found which species differ between the groups. The next question is a practical one: if we only had a stool sample, how well could we tell whether the person has CRC? This is a prediction question, and machine learning is the usual tool for it. The outcome we predict can be anything we know about the samples, for example a disease, a treatment response or a diet; in our study, it is the disease.

    Load packages and data

    R 

    library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(mikropml)
library(ggplot2)

    R 

    tse <- readRDS(file.path("data", "tse_processed.rds"))

    What is machine learning?

    So far we have asked whether the groups differ. Machine learning asks whether we can predict the group of a new sample. A few terms:

    Term Meaning In our data
    Outcome What we want to predict disease: CRC or healthy
    Features What we use to predict it The abundances of the taxa
    Model A set of rules learned from the data A random forest
    Hyperparameter A setting of the model that is chosen before training, not learned from the data mtry of the random forest (see below)
    Training data The samples the model learns from 80 % of the samples
    Test data Samples kept aside to check the model The other 20 %

    Why keep test data aside?

    A flexible model can learn the training data by heart, including its random noise. It then looks perfect on the training data but fails on new samples. This is called overfitting. To get an honest estimate of how well the model works, we test it on samples that it has never seen.

    The data is used like this:

    1. The samples are split into training data (80 %) and test data (20 %).
    2. On the training data, the model is tuned with cross-validation: the training data is split into 5 parts (folds), the model is trained on 4 and checked on the 5th, and this is repeated so that each fold is used for checking once. This gives the cross-validation (CV) performance. Tuning means that this is done for several values of the hyperparameters, and the values with the best CV performance are kept.
    3. The final model is checked once on the test data. This gives the test performance.

    Measuring performance: AUC

    For each sample, the model gives a probability of CRC. The AUC (area under the ROC curve) measures how well these probabilities rank the samples:

    • AUC = 1: every CRC sample gets a higher probability than every healthy sample.
    • AUC = 0.5: no better than flipping a coin.

    To turn the probabilities into a yes/no prediction, we need a cut-off, for example “CRC if the probability is above 0.5”. The ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic) shows what happens for every possible cut-off: how many of the CRC samples are found (the sensitivity), against how many of the healthy samples are wrongly called CRC (the false positive rate). The AUC is the area under this curve, so it does not depend on one chosen cut-off. Another common measure, the accuracy, is the share of samples predicted correctly at one cut-off.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Training and test data

    A student trains a model on all 60 samples and then checks it on the same samples. The model gets an AUC of 1.0. Should the student be happy? Why or why not?

    No. The model was checked on the samples it learned from, so it may have memorized them (overfitting). The AUC of 1.0 says nothing about how the model works for new people. The model must be checked on samples it has not seen, such as a separate test set.

    Prepare the data

    We use the same taxa as in the differential abundance episode: the species that are found in at least 10 % of the samples.

    R 

    tse_prevalent <- subsetByPrevalent(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance",
    detection = 0.001, prevalence = 0.1
)

    We use the raw counts as features: a random forest splits each feature into “high” and “low” values, so it does not need normally distributed or transformed data.

    Train a random forest

    A random forest is a collection of many decision trees. Each tree asks a series of questions such as “is the count of Prevotella copri above 10 000?” and ends with a prediction. The forest predicts by majority vote of its trees.

    The most important hyperparameter of a random forest is mtry: the number of randomly chosen features that each question in a tree can pick from. A small mtry makes the trees more different from each other; a large mtry makes each tree stronger on its own. The best value depends on the data, so we let cross-validation choose it.

    The mikropml function run_ml() works directly with a TreeSE. We give it the outcome as a column of colData (outcome_colname) and the features as an abundance table (assay.type). It then does all the steps from above: it splits the data into training and test data, tunes mtry with 5-fold cross-validation (kfold = 5, repeated cv_times = 5 times with different folds), and tests the final model. The seed makes the random split reproducible.

    R 

    rf_results <- run_ml(
    tse_prevalent, method = "rf", outcome_colname = "disease",
    assay.type = "counts", kfold = 5, cv_times = 5, seed = 123
)

    The mikropml functions get_hp_performance() and plot_hp_performance() show the CV AUC for each value of mtry that was tried:

    R 

    hp <- get_hp_performance(rf_results$trained_model)
plot_hp_performance(hp$dat, mtry, AUC)

    Result: all values of mtry give a similar CV AUC (note the narrow range of the y-axis), and run_ml() kept mtry = 5, the value with the highest CV AUC.

    Evaluate the model

    The performance is stored in rf_results$performance. The two most important columns are the cross-validation AUC of the chosen model and the test AUC:

    R 

    rf_results$performance[, c("cv_metric_AUC", "AUC")]

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 1 × 2
  cv_metric_AUC   AUC
          <dbl> <dbl>
1         0.906     1

    The mikropml function calc_model_sensspec() predicts the test data with the trained model and calculates the sensitivity and false positive rate for every cut-off. We plot them as a ROC curve. The dashed line is a model that guesses at random (AUC = 0.5):

    R 

    sensspec <- calc_model_sensspec(
    rf_results$trained_model, rf_results$test_data, "disease"
)

    OUTPUT 

    Using 'disease' as the outcome column.

    R 

    ggplot(sensspec, aes(x = fpr, y = sensitivity)) +
    geom_step() +
    geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(x = "False positive rate", y = "Sensitivity")

    Result: the cross-validation AUC is 0.91, and the test AUC is 1. The gut microbiome predicts CRC very well in this study.

    The CV AUC was used to choose mtry, so it is slightly optimistic. The test data was not used for any choice, so the test AUC is the honest estimate.

    But the test set contains only 12 samples. With so few samples, a single lucky or unlucky split can change the test AUC a lot. Challenge 2 explores this.

    run_ml() takes a few seconds. It loads the caret package, which masks some functions, for example mia::cluster(). This does not matter in this episode, but in a session that also uses clustering, call such functions with mia:: in front.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: How reliable is one test set?

    The split into training and test data is random, and it is set by seed. Let’s see how much the test AUC depends on it.

    1. Train the same random forest three more times, with seed = 4, seed = 5 and seed = 6. Store the results as rf_4, rf_5 and rf_6.
    2. Combine the performance tables of the four models (rf_results and the three new ones) with rbind(), and plot them with the mikropml function plot_model_performance().
    3. What are the smallest and largest test AUCs? What does this tell you about reporting the AUC of a single split?
    4. Do the cross-validation AUCs vary as much? Why might that be?

    R 

    rf_4 <- run_ml(
    tse_prevalent, method = "rf", outcome_colname = "disease",
    assay.type = "counts", kfold = 5, cv_times = 5, seed = 4
)
rf_5 <- run_ml(
    tse_prevalent, method = "rf", outcome_colname = "disease",
    assay.type = "counts", kfold = 5, cv_times = 5, seed = 5
)
rf_6 <- run_ml(
    tse_prevalent, method = "rf", outcome_colname = "disease",
    assay.type = "counts", kfold = 5, cv_times = 5, seed = 6
)
performance <- rbind(
    rf_results$performance, rf_4$performance,
    rf_5$performance, rf_6$performance
)
performance[, c("seed", "cv_metric_AUC", "AUC")]

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 4 × 3
   seed cv_metric_AUC   AUC
  <dbl>         <dbl> <dbl>
1   123         0.906 1
2     4         0.958 0.833
3     5         0.919 1
4     6         0.978 0.722

    R 

    plot_model_performance(performance)
    1. The test AUC ranges from 0.72 to 1. A single split of a small dataset can make a model look perfect or mediocre by chance. Report the performance over many splits (for example the median and range), not from one split. In practice, people use many more splits, for example 100; the mikropml documentation shows how to run them efficiently.
    2. The cross-validation AUCs vary less (from 0.91 to 0.98), because each one is an average over 25 folds (5 folds, repeated 5 times) that together use all 48 training samples, while the test AUC comes from only 12 samples.

    Which taxa matter most?

    A model that predicts well is useful, but we also want to know which features it relies on. A random forest measures the importance of each feature: how much the questions about this feature help the trees to separate CRC from healthy samples, summed over all trees. mikropml trains the model with the caret package, so we get the importances with the caret function varImp(). It scales them from 0 (least important) to 100 (most important) and prints the most important features first:

    R 

    importance <- caret::varImp(rf_results$trained_model)
importance

    OUTPUT 

    rf variable importance

  only 20 most important variables shown (out of 94)

                                        Overall
species-Roseburia_faecis                 100.00
species-Prevotella_copri                  67.75
species-Odoribacter_splanchnicus          54.15
species-_rectale                          50.03
species-Bacteroides_fragilis              44.09
species-Flavonifractor_plautii            42.44
species-Parabacteroides_distasonis        42.16
species-Ruthenibacterium_lactatiformans   40.52
species-Ligilactobacillus_ruminis         39.92
species-Faecalibacterium_prausnitzii      36.55
species-Bacteroides_thetaiotaomicron      31.23
species-Bifidobacterium_adolescentis      30.58
species-Methanobrevibacter_smithii        29.87
species-Megasphaera_elsdenii              27.18
species-Alistipes_shahii                  24.88
species-Escherichia_coli                  23.32
species-Phocaeicola_vulgatus              20.12
species-Parabacteroides_merdae            19.54
species-Akkermansia_muciniphila           19.42
species-Bacteroides_intestinalis          18.99

    caret also provides a ggplot() method for this object. We plot the ten most important species:

    R 

    ggplot(importance, top = 10)

    Result: the most important species is Roseburia faecis, followed by Prevotella copri and Odoribacter splanchnicus. Compare them with the differential abundance results of episode 8: many of the same species appear in both. Two very different methods point to the same bacteria.

    Callout

    Other importance measures

    mikropml can also calculate permutation importance with run_ml(..., find_feature_importance = TRUE): it shuffles one feature at a time in the test data and measures how much the test AUC drops. With only 12 test samples, this estimate is very noisy, so we use the importance from the random forest itself. See the mikropml documentation.

    Callout

    Importance is not a difference

    Feature importance tells us that a taxon helps the model to predict, but not in which direction: it does not say whether the taxon is higher in CRC or in healthy people. For that, look at the differential abundance results or plot the taxon by group with plotBoxplot().

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: A different model

    mikropml supports other models too. A popular one is a regularized logistic regression, method = "glmnet". Unlike a random forest, it combines the features in a weighted sum, so it works best when the features are on a similar scale.

    1. Prepare the relative abundances of tse_prevalent with the mikropml function preprocess_data() (outcome_colname = "disease", assay.type = "relabundance"). By default, it centres and scales each feature and removes features that carry no information. It adds the result to the TreeSE as a new table called preprocessed.
    2. Train a glmnet model on the preprocessed table with the same settings as before.
    3. Compare its cross-validation AUC with the random forest.

    R 

    tse_glm <- preprocess_data(
    tse_prevalent, outcome_colname = "disease", assay.type = "relabundance"
)
assayNames(tse_glm)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "counts"       "relabundance" "rclr"         "preprocessed"

    R 

    glm_results <- run_ml(
    tse_glm, method = "glmnet", outcome_colname = "disease",
    assay.type = "preprocessed", kfold = 5, cv_times = 5, seed = 123
)
glm_results$performance[, c("cv_metric_AUC", "AUC")]

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 1 × 2
  cv_metric_AUC   AUC
          <dbl> <dbl>
1         0.884     1

    The glmnet model has a cross-validation AUC of 0.88, compared with 0.91 for the random forest. Both predict CRC well. With only 60 samples, a small difference between the models could change with another split. glmnet is much faster, which matters for large datasets.

    If preprocess_data() removes features, it stores the result as an alternative experiment instead, and you give run_ml() also altexp = "preprocessed". See the Machine learning chapter of OMA.

    Challenge

    Challenge 4: Genus level

    Does the model work as well at the genus level?

    1. Agglomerate the data to the genus level with agglomerateByRank().
    2. Filter and train a random forest as above.
    3. Compare the cross-validation AUC with the species-level model.

    R 

    tse_genus <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "genus")
tse_genus <- transformAssay(
    tse_genus, assay.type = "counts", method = "relabundance"
)
tse_genus <- subsetByPrevalent(
    tse_genus, assay.type = "relabundance",
    detection = 0.001, prevalence = 0.1
)
genus_results <- run_ml(
    tse_genus, method = "rf", outcome_colname = "disease",
    assay.type = "counts", kfold = 5, cv_times = 5, seed = 123
)
genus_results$performance[, c("cv_metric_AUC", "AUC")]

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 1 × 2
  cv_metric_AUC   AUC
          <dbl> <dbl>
1         0.931 0.944

    With 52 genera, the cross-validation AUC is 0.93, about the same as with species (0.91). The signal is strong at both levels.

    Challenge

    Challenge 5: Is it really the disease?

    In our study, most people from Kerala have CRC (episode 4).

    1. Make a table of location against disease.
    2. Imagine a very simple “model”: predict CRC for everyone from Kerala and healthy for everyone from Bhopal. What share of the people would it classify correctly?
    3. What does this mean for our microbiome model?

    R 

    location_table <- table(tse$location, tse$disease)
location_table

    OUTPUT 

    
         CRC healthy
  Bhopal  15      26
  Kerala  15       4

    R 

    correct <- location_table["Kerala", "CRC"] + location_table["Bhopal", "healthy"]
correct / ncol(tse)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 0.6833333
    1. The simple rule classifies 68 % of the people correctly, without looking at any bacteria.
    2. Part of what the model learns could be the difference between Bhopal and Kerala rather than the disease. The microbiome model is much better than the location alone, but to be sure, it should be tested on new people, ideally from other places, or trained within one place only.
    Callout

    Before trusting a prediction model

    • Small data. With 60 samples, performance estimates are uncertain. Report results over many splits.
    • Independent validation. A model should be tested on an independent cohort, collected by other people in another place. Models often perform worse there.
    • Confounding. If the groups differ in other ways (location, age, medication), the model may learn those differences instead of the disease.

    See the Machine learning chapter of OMA.

    Key Points
    • Machine learning asks how well we can predict an outcome, such as a disease, from features, such as taxon abundances.
    • Always evaluate a model on samples it has not seen: cross-validation on the training data and a separate test set.
    • Hyperparameters, such as mtry of a random forest, are chosen by cross-validation on the training data only.
    • mikropml works directly with a TreeSE: run_ml() trains, tunes and tests a model in one call, and preprocess_data() prepares the data when a model needs it. Random forests work on raw counts.
    • The AUC measures how well the predictions separate the groups. With a small test set, it varies a lot between random splits.
    • Feature importance shows which taxa the model relies on. In our study, many of them, such as Roseburia faecis, also differ in abundance.
    • Confounders and small sample sizes can make a model look better than it is; independent validation is needed.

    Content from Capstone: analyse a new dataset

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 60 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • Can I run a complete microbiome analysis on my own?
    • How do I report the results of a microbiome analysis?

    Objectives

    • Explore and prepare a new microbiome dataset.
    • Compare alpha diversity, beta diversity and the abundance of single taxa between two groups, while taking a second variable into account.
    • Interpret results that differ from those of the main study, including results that are not significant.
    • Summarize an analysis in a short written report.

    Where are we?

    You now know every step of the workflow: import, exploration and preparation, alpha diversity, beta diversity and differential abundance. In this episode, you run the whole workflow on your own, on a dataset you have not seen before. The tasks below guide you. Try each task yourself before you open its solution, and use the earlier episodes as a reference.

    Plan about 40 minutes for Tasks 1–5 and 10 minutes for the report in Task 7. Task 6 and the optional part of Task 3 are extras for those who have time. If you get stuck on a task, open its solution and continue: the report matters more than solving every task alone.

    The dataset

    The mia package includes several example datasets. We use Tengeler2020, from a study of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (Tengeler et al. 2020). The researchers transferred gut microbiota from people with ADHD and from healthy controls into germ-free mice, to test whether the microbiota can affect the brain. The dataset holds 27 gut microbiota profiles. For each sample, we know:

    • patient_status: whether the microbiota came from a person with ADHD or from a control;
    • cohort: in which of three experimental cohorts the sample was processed.

    Unlike our main study, these data come from 16S amplicon sequencing (episode 2). The table holds real read counts, and the taxa are genus-level groups of reads (for example Bacteroides_1, Bacteroides_2).

    The research question is:

    Does the gut microbiota of people with ADHD differ from that of controls, and which bacteria differ?

    Load packages and data

    R 

    library(mia)
library(miaViz)
library(maaslin3)

    R 

    data("Tengeler2020", package = "mia")
tse <- Tengeler2020
tse

    OUTPUT 

    class: TreeSummarizedExperiment
dim: 151 27
metadata(0):
assays(1): counts
rownames(151): Bacteroides Bacteroides_1 ... Parabacteroides_8
  Unidentified_Lachnospiraceae_14
rowData names(6): Kingdom Phylum ... Family Genus
colnames(27): A110 A12 ... A35 A38
colData names(4): patient_status cohort patient_status_vs_cohort
  sample_name
reducedDimNames(0):
mainExpName: NULL
altExpNames(0):
rowLinks: a LinkDataFrame (151 rows)
rowTree: 1 phylo tree(s) (151 leaves)
colLinks: NULL
colTree: NULL

    The data is already a TreeSE, with a phylogenetic tree. Note that the taxonomic ranks in rowData are capitalized: Phylum, Family, Genus.

    Challenge

    Task 1: Who is in the study?

    1. How many samples are there from ADHD donors and from controls?
    2. How are the two groups spread over the three cohorts? Make a table and a bar plot.
    3. Could the cohort be a confounder, as the location was in our main study?

    R 

    table(tse$patient_status, tse$cohort)

    OUTPUT 

    
          Cohort_1 Cohort_2 Cohort_3
  ADHD           4        5        4
  Control        6        5        3

    R 

    plotBarplot(tse, col.var = "cohort", fill.by = "patient_status")
    1. There are 13 ADHD samples and 14 control samples.
    2. Every cohort has both ADHD and control samples, in roughly equal numbers.
    3. The cohort is not strongly linked to the patient status, so it is a much smaller problem than the location was in the main study. Still, samples processed together can be more similar to each other (a batch effect), so it is good practice to include cohort in the models.
    Challenge

    Task 2: Explore and prepare the data

    1. Calculate the library size of each sample, store it in colData, and plot it with plotHistogram(). How much do the library sizes differ?
    2. Add relative abundances with transformAssay().
    3. Plot the composition of each sample at phylum level, split by patient_status. Which phyla dominate?
    4. Which five taxa are the most abundant?
    5. Add rclr values with transformAssay(). Why do we add them only after the composition plot?

    R 

    tse$library_size <- colSums(assay(tse, "counts"))
summary(tse$library_size)

    OUTPUT 

       Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
   1772   11804   16745   17997   21502   40584

    R 

    plotHistogram(tse, col.var = "library_size", binwidth = 2000)

    R 

    tse <- transformAssay(tse, assay.type = "counts", method = "relabundance")

    R 

    plotAbundance(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance", group = "Phylum",
    col.var = "patient_status", facet.cols = TRUE, scales = "free_x"
)

    R 

    getTop(tse, top = 5)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "Bacteroides"     "Bacteroides_1"   "Parabacteroides" "Bacteroides_2"
[5] "Akkermansia"

    R 

    tse <- transformAssay(tse, assay.type = "counts", method = "rclr")
assayNames(tse)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "counts"       "relabundance" "rclr"
    1. The largest library is about 23 times larger than the smallest. With real read counts, such differences matter for richness (see Task 3).
    2. Bacteroidetes dominate (on average 65 % of the community), followed by Firmicutes (27 %) and Verrucomicrobia (6 %). By eye, the two groups look similar. This dataset uses the older phylum name Bacteroidetes for the phylum that is called Bacteroidota in our main study. plotAbundance() may warn about removed rows; as in episode 5, this is harmless.
    3. Mostly Bacteroides groups, Parabacteroides and Akkermansia.
    4. With group = "Phylum", plotAbundance() agglomerates all tables to phylum level, by summing. Summed rclr values are meaningless, and plotAbundance() would warn about them. Remember the rule from episode 5: agglomerate first, then transform.
    Challenge

    Task 3: Alpha diversity

    1. Calculate observed richness, Shannon diversity and Faith’s phylogenetic diversity with addAlpha().
    2. Plot the Shannon diversity by patient_status, and test the difference with the Wilcoxon test. Do the same for the other two indices.
    3. Optional: this is amplicon data with real read counts, and the library sizes differ a lot. Calculate a rarefied richness with the sample and niter arguments of addAlpha() (rarefy to the smallest library size). Does the conclusion change?

    R 

    tse <- addAlpha(
    tse, assay.type = "counts",
    index = c("observed_richness", "shannon_diversity", "faith_diversity")
)

    R 

    plotBoxplot(tse, col.var = "shannon_diversity", x = "patient_status")

    R 

    p_shannon <- wilcox.test(shannon_diversity ~ patient_status, data = colData(tse))$p.value
p_richness <- wilcox.test(observed_richness ~ patient_status, data = colData(tse))$p.value
p_faith <- wilcox.test(faith_diversity ~ patient_status, data = colData(tse))$p.value
c(shannon = p_shannon, richness = p_richness, faith = p_faith)

    OUTPUT 

      shannon  richness     faith
0.4879480 0.9333796 0.9809717

    R 

    tse <- addAlpha(
    tse, assay.type = "counts", index = "observed_richness",
    sample = min(tse$library_size), niter = 10, name = "richness_rarefied"
)
p_rarefied <- wilcox.test(richness_rarefied ~ patient_status, data = colData(tse))$p.value
p_rarefied

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 0.8954888
    1. None of the indices differ between the groups (Shannon p = 0.49, richness p = 0.93, Faith p = 0.98).
    2. The rarefied richness does not differ either (p = 0.9). The conclusion is the same. Rarefying makes the richness values comparable across samples with different sequencing depths, which is why it is common for amplicon data.
    Challenge

    Task 4: Beta diversity

    1. Make a PCoA with Bray–Curtis dissimilarity, and colour it by patient_status. Then colour it by cohort.
    2. Test with PERMANOVA whether the composition differs by patient_status, taking cohort into account (formula = x ~ patient_status + cohort). Add by = "margin", so that each variable is tested while the other is taken into account.
    3. Check the homogeneity of the group spreads. Can you trust the PERMANOVA result?

    R 

    tse <- addMDS(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance", method = "bray", name = "PCoA_BC"
)
plotOrdination(tse, "PCoA_BC", colour.by = "patient_status")

    R 

    plotOrdination(tse, "PCoA_BC", colour.by = "cohort")

    R 

    permanova <- getPERMANOVA(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance", method = "bray",
    formula = x ~ patient_status + cohort, by = "margin"
)
permanova$permanova

    OUTPUT 

    Permutation test for adonis under reduced model
Marginal effects of terms
Permutation: free
Number of permutations: 999

adonis2(formula = formula, data = data, method = ..1, by = by, na.action = na.action)
               Df SumOfSqs      R2      F Pr(>F)
patient_status  1   0.3790 0.06819 1.7880  0.104
cohort          2   0.3212 0.05780 0.7578  0.686
Residual       23   4.8748 0.87721
Total          26   5.5572 1.00000

    R 

    permanova$homogeneity

    OUTPUT 

                   Df      Sum Sq      Mean Sq          F N.Perm Pr(>F)
patient_status  1 0.001208740 0.0012087403 0.08912270    999  0.754
cohort          2 0.001793416 0.0008967079 0.07260098    999  0.927
               Total variance Explained variance
patient_status      0.3402751        0.003552244
cohort              0.2982218        0.006013699
    1. ADHD and control samples are found on both sides of the first axis, so the groups overlap a lot. A tight group of ADHD samples lies at the bottom of the plot; it contains samples from two cohorts. The cohorts are spread over the whole plot.
    2. Patient status explains 7 % of the differences between samples, but this is not significant (p = 0.1). The cohort is not significant either (p = 0.69).
    3. The spreads do not differ (p = 0.75), so the assumption of PERMANOVA holds. We find no significant difference in overall composition, even though some ADHD samples form their own group in the plot.
    Challenge

    Task 5: Differential abundance and prevalence

    1. Make Control the reference level of patient_status, and turn cohort into a factor.
    2. Keep the taxa with a relative abundance of at least 0.1 % in at least 10 % of the samples.
    3. Run MaAsLin 3 with formula = ~ patient_status + cohort and output = "maaslin3_output_tengeler".
    4. Which taxa differ in abundance between ADHD and controls (q < 0.05)? In which direction? Do any taxa differ in prevalence?
    5. Plot the relative abundance of the taxa that differ in abundance by patient_status.

    R 

    tse$patient_status <- factor(tse$patient_status, levels = c("Control", "ADHD"))
tse$cohort <- factor(tse$cohort)
tse_prevalent <- subsetByPrevalent(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance",
    detection = 0.001, prevalence = 0.1
)
nrow(tse_prevalent)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 145

    R 

    fit <- maaslin3(
    tse_prevalent,
    formula = ~ patient_status + cohort,
    output = "maaslin3_output_tengeler",
    plot_summary_plot = FALSE,
    plot_associations = FALSE,
    verbosity = "ERROR"
)
res <- fit$fit_data_abundance$results
res <- res[res$metadata == "patient_status", ]
sig <- res[res$qval_individual < 0.05 & !is.na(res$qval_individual), ]
sig[, c("feature", "coef", "qval_individual")]

    OUTPUT 

                feature      coef qval_individual
1       Coprobacter  2.984114      0.01305400
2 Subdoligranulum_1 -2.378099      0.04089055

    R 

    res_pa <- fit$fit_data_prevalence$results
res_pa <- res_pa[res_pa$metadata == "patient_status", ]
sig_pa <- res_pa[res_pa$qval_individual < 0.05 & !is.na(res_pa$qval_individual), ]
sig_pa[, c("feature", "coef", "qval_individual")]

    OUTPUT 

    [1] feature         coef            qval_individual
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

    R 

    plotBoxplot(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance", x = "patient_status",
    features = sig$feature, facet.by = "rownames"
)
    1. 2 of the 145 taxa differ in abundance. More abundant in ADHD: Coprobacter. Less abundant in ADHD: Subdoligranulum_1. 0 taxa differ in prevalence.
    2. The box plots show the differences, but also a large overlap between the groups and many zeros. With only 27 samples, treat these taxa as candidates for further study.
    Challenge

    Task 6 (optional): Clustering

    Cluster the samples into two groups with hierarchical clustering on the rclr values, as in episode 7. Do the clusters match the patient status?

    R 

    library(bluster)
tse <- addCluster(
    tse, assay.type = "rclr", by = "cols",
    HclustParam(method = "ward.D2", cut.params = list(k = 2))
)
table(tse$cluster, tse$patient_status)

    OUTPUT 

    
    Control ADHD
  1       8    5
  2       6    8

    The clusters do not follow the patient status. This agrees with the PCoA and PERMANOVA: the main structure in these data is not related to ADHD.

    Challenge

    Task 7: Write a short report

    Write a short report (about half a page) of your analysis, as you would for a lab meeting. Answer the research question and include:

    1. The data: what was measured, in how many samples, in which groups.
    2. The methods: which tables, indices, distances and tests you used, and why.
    3. The results: one sentence each for alpha diversity, beta diversity and differential abundance, with the key numbers.
    4. The limitations: for example the sample size, the cohorts, and what a non-significant result does and does not mean.
    5. One figure that best supports your conclusion.

    In a workshop, share your report in the shared notes and compare it with those of other learners.

    An example report:

    We analysed 16S amplicon profiles of 27 gut microbiota samples from a mouse study in which microbiota from people with ADHD (n = 13) and from controls (n = 14) were transferred to germ-free mice, in three cohorts. Alpha diversity (observed richness, Shannon and Faith’s index; Wilcoxon tests) did not differ between the groups (Shannon p = 0.49), also after rarefying. The overall composition did not differ either (Bray–Curtis PERMANOVA adjusted for cohort: R² = 0.07, p = 0.1; group spreads did not differ). MaAsLin 3, adjusted for cohort, found 2 of 145 taxa that differed in abundance and 0 that differed in prevalence (q < 0.05). The study is small, so it can only detect large differences: the lack of a significant difference in diversity or composition does not prove that there is none. Any taxa found are candidates that need confirmation in a larger study.

    Callout

    Not every study finds a difference

    In our main study, CRC and healthy people differed clearly in diversity, composition and many taxa. In this dataset, most tests are not significant. This is a normal and useful result. Report it honestly, together with the sample size, rather than searching for a test that gives a small p-value.

    Key Points
    • The same workflow (explore, alpha diversity, beta diversity, differential abundance) works for new datasets, including amplicon data.
    • With real read counts and very different library sizes, rarefaction is an option for richness.
    • Include technical variables such as the cohort or batch in the models.
    • Non-significant results are results too. Report them together with the sample size and the limitations.
    • A short written report forces you to state the question, the methods, the results and the limitations clearly.

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 15 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What did we learn about our study?
    • Where can I learn more?

    Objectives

    • Summarize the analysis workflow of this lesson.
    • Find resources for further learning.

    What we did

    We have gone through the data object, data processing and statistical analysis steps of the microbiome data science workflow. We started with one question: is the gut microbiome of people with colorectal cancer different from that of healthy people, and which bacteria differ? Step by step, we found an answer:

    Episode Step What we learned about the study
    4 Import The data fits into one TreeSummarizedExperiment. Most healthy people come from Bhopal.
    5 Explore and prepare Library sizes differ between samples. Prevotella dominates many healthy samples.
    6 Alpha diversity CRC patients have higher diversity, partly because many healthy samples are dominated by Prevotella and are therefore less even.
    7 Beta diversity and clustering The overall composition of the two groups differs, also when the location is taken into account. The samples fall into a Prevotella and a non-Prevotella community type.
    8 Differential abundance and prevalence Several species differ. Prevotella copri and butyrate producers such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii are less abundant in CRC. Others differ in how often they are present, for example Flavonifractor plautii, which is found much more often in CRC. Others differ in how often they are present, for example Flavonifractor plautii, which is found much more often in CRC.
    9 Machine learning The microbiome predicts CRC well, but with only 60 people the estimate is uncertain and an independent cohort is needed.
    10 Capstone The same workflow works on a new dataset, even when it finds few differences.

    The same workflow works for most microbiome studies: import the data, explore and prepare it, analyse alpha diversity, beta diversity and differential abundance, and then go further with clustering, machine learning or multi-omics.

    Where to go next

    This lesson covered the basics. The online book Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis (OMA) goes deeper into each topic and covers many more. Good places to continue:

    • Your own data: importing data from QIIME 2, MetaPhlAn, mothur, BIOM files and phyloseq objects (Import chapter).
    • More about each step: quality control, other transformations, other diversity indices and distances, rarefaction, other differential abundance methods, and other clustering and machine learning methods.
    • Multi-omics: combining the microbiome with other data types, such as metabolites, is the topic of the follow-up multi-omics lesson. It covers MultiAssayExperiment, exploratory methods (Mantel test, MiRKAT, pairwise associations), unsupervised methods (joint RPCA, MOFA) and supervised methods (IntegratedLearner, DIABLO).
    • Your own analysis: apply the workflow to your own data, and report it in a reproducible way, for example with Quarto.

    Other resources:

    • OMA framework: the R/Bioconductor packages for microbiome data science.
    • Training slides: slides on many microbiome analysis topics.
    • Bioconductor support site: ask questions about Bioconductor packages, using the tags mia or miaViz.
    Key Points
    • A typical microbiome analysis goes from import and preparation to alpha diversity, beta diversity and differential abundance.
    • These three analyses are what most studies report. They are sometimes enough on their own, and they are always the first steps before more advanced analyses.
    • The OMA book is the place to continue learning, and the follow-up multi-omics lesson shows how to combine the microbiome with other data types.
